ai.literal: Even when thinking of, because it creates unceasing great joy, love is sweeter than liquor.
ai.translation: Because it yields an endless, great joy even when one merely thinks of it, love is sweeter than wine.
ai.modern: மனதால் நினைத்துப் பார்த்தாலும் நீங்காத பெருமகிழ்ச்சியைத் தருவதால், கள்ளைக் குடிப்பதை விடக் காமம் இனிமையானது.
ai.explanation: In this couplet, the pining lover compares the pleasure of love to the intoxication of liquor. While liquor only gives pleasure when it is physically consumed, love has the unique power to give immense, unceasing joy through mere memory and contemplation. The word 'uḷḷiṉum' (even when thinking) highlights that physical presence is not required to experience this bliss. Therefore, love is declared to be far sweeter and superior to liquor.

ai.literal: How much, in one way, why is it sweet, behold, love, when if they think of those whom they themselves love, that which comes is a certain joy!
ai.translation: Behold, how sweet is love! For if one merely thinks of the beloved, it brings such an exquisite joy.
ai.modern: நாம் விரும்பும் காதலரை நினைக்கும்போதே இன்பம் தருகிறது என்றால், காமம் எவ்வளவு இனிமையானது என்று பாருங்கள்!
ai.explanation: In this couplet, the heroine marvels at the nature of love. She expresses that love is incredibly sweet because even the mere thought of the beloved brings immense joy. The word 'நினைப்ப' (when thinking of) highlights that physical presence is not required to experience the pleasure of love; memory alone is sufficient. The phrase 'வருவது ஒன்று' refers to the unique, incomparable happiness that arises from these thoughts.

ai.literal: Like he who thinks, does he not think? I wonder; the sneeze, like budding, disappears.
ai.translation: Does my lover seem to think of me, but then stop? For my sneeze, which was about to burst forth, has subsided and disappeared.
ai.modern: அவர் என்னை நினைப்பவர் போலத் தொடங்கிப் பின் நினையாமல் விட்டுவிடுகிறாரோ? ஏனெனில், வரவிருந்த தும்மல் அரும்புவது போலத் தோன்றிப் பின் அடங்கிவிடுகிறது.
ai.explanation: This couplet draws on the traditional Tamil belief that a sneeze is triggered when a loved one thinks of you. The heroine feels a sneeze beginning to form in her nose, which is described beautifully as 'சினைப்பது' (budding like a flower). However, the sneeze suddenly fades away ('கெடும்') without happening. She wonders if her distant lover started to think of her, but then immediately stopped, causing her physical sneeze to abort mid-way.

ai.literal: I too exist-perhaps in his heart? In my heart, oh, exists-indeed he!
ai.translation: Do I even exist in his heart? In my heart, oh, he constantly dwells!
ai.modern: அவருடைய நெஞ்சத்தில் நானும் இருக்கிறேனா? ஆனால், என் நெஞ்சத்தில் அவரோ எப்போதும் இருக்கிறார்!
ai.explanation: The heroine, suffering from the pain of separation, wonders if she occupies any place at all in her lover's thoughts. She uses the doubtful particle 'கொல்' to question if she exists in his heart. In contrast, she uses the emphatic 'ஏ' and an exclamatory sigh 'ஓஒ' to state that he is permanently and vividly present in her own heart. This contrast beautifully highlights the vulnerability and one-sided intensity of her longing during separation.

ai.literal: In their heart me banishing those who did, do they not feel shame, in my heart unceasingly coming?
ai.translation: Are they not ashamed, those who have barred me from their own heart, to keep coming unceasingly into mine?
ai.modern: தம்முடைய நெஞ்சத்தில் என்னை வரவிடாமல் தடுத்துக்கொண்டவர், என்னுடைய நெஞ்சத்தில் இடைவிடாமல் வந்து கொண்டிருப்பதற்கு வெட்கப்பட மாட்டாரா?
ai.explanation: The heroine, suffering in separation, speaks of her beloved who has left her. She notes that he has locked her out of his own thoughts and heart, yet he constantly and unceasingly enters her heart as a persistent memory. She wonders, with a touch of irony, if he feels no shame in intruding so relentlessly into her mind while denying her a place in his. The contrast between 'their heart' and 'my heart' highlights the painful asymmetry of their love during separation.

ai.literal: Otherwise, why am I alive indeed? With him, I, the spent days, remembering, am alive.
ai.translation: Otherwise, how indeed do I survive? I only remain alive by remembering the days I spent with him.

ai.explanation: The heroine, suffering from the pain of separation, explains how she manages to stay alive. She asks how she could possibly survive otherwise, revealing that her existence depends entirely on memory. It is only by constantly remembering (உள்ள) the happy days (நாள்) she spent (உற்ற) in union with her lover (அவரொடு) that she keeps her breath. Without these sweet recollections to sustain her, she would have perished from grief.

words.gloss: even if I think of him

ai.literal: If I forget, what will I become? Alas! Forgetting I do not know; even if I think of him, my heart burns.
ai.translation: If I were to forget him, what would become of me? But alas, I do not even know how to forget! And yet, even when I merely think of him, my heart burns.
ai.modern: அவரை நான் மறந்தால் எனக்கு என்ன நேரிடும்? ஆனால் எனக்கு மறக்கவே தெரியாது; அவரை நினைத்தாலும் என் நெஞ்சம் சுடுகிறது.
ai.explanation: The heroine describes her helpless state of longing during separation. She wonders what would happen to her if she could forget her lover, but immediately admits that she does not even know how to forget him ('மறப்பு அறியேன்'). Ironically, even when she does not forget and merely thinks of him ('உள்ளினும்'), the memory is so intense that it burns her heart ('உள்ளம் சுடும்'). She is trapped in a state where neither forgetting is possible, nor is remembering comforting.

words.gloss: even if I think of him

ai.literal: However much [I] think [of him], [he] does not get angry; is that not indeed the special favor that [my] lover does [for me]?
ai.translation: However much I think of him, he does not get angry; is that not indeed the special favor my beloved does for me?
ai.modern: நான் எவ்வளவு நினைத்தாலும் என் காதலர் என் மீது கோபப்பட மாட்டார்; அதுவே அவர் எனக்குச் செய்யும் சிறந்த அன்பு அல்லவா?
ai.explanation: In this couplet, the heroine, enduring the pain of separation, finds comfort in her thoughts of her beloved. She notes that no matter how constantly or intensely she thinks of him, he never grows angry or annoyed at being summoned in her mind. She perceives this enduring sweetness and lack of resentment in her thoughts as a special act of kindness and favor from her lover. The word 'kāyār' (does not get angry) highlights the gentle nature of the beloved, who remains a source of comfort rather than irritation, even when her mind is entirely consumed by him.

ai.literal: Will perish my sweet life, 'different we are not' he who says, his love's absence greatly remembering.
ai.translation: My sweet life will perish as I think intensely of the lack of love shown by him who once said, 'We are not two separate beings'.
ai.modern: நாம் இருவரும் வேறு வேறானவர் அல்லர் என்று கூறிய காதலரின் அன்பில்லாத தன்மையை மிகவும் நினைத்து எனது இனிய உயிர் அழிகிறது.
ai.explanation: The heroine is suffering deeply in separation from her lover. She recalls his past promises when he used to say they were one soul and not separate individuals ('வேறு அல்லம் என்பார்'). Now, his prolonged absence feels like a complete lack of love and grace ('அளியின்மை'). Constantly and intensely dwelling on this painful contrast ('ஆற்ற நினைந்து') is slowly destroying her very life ('விளியும் என் இன்னுயிர்').

do not set / do not disappear

ai.literal: Without leaving him who departed, with my eyes to see, do not set, live long, O Moon!
ai.translation: May you live long, O Moon! Do not set yet, so that I may behold with my own eyes him who departed from me but has never left my heart.
ai.modern: என் நெஞ்சை விட்டு நீங்காமல் பிரிந்து சென்றவரை என் கண்களால் காணும் வரை, நிலவே! நீ மறையாமல் இருப்பாயாக; நீ வாழ்க!
ai.explanation: In this verse, the pining heroine addresses the moon. She speaks of her lover as one who has departed physically but has never left her thoughts. She pleads with the moon not to set just yet, wishing it a long life, so that she may have enough light to see him with her own eyes. The use of the lengthened phonetic forms 'விடாஅது' and 'படாஅதி' emphasizes her deep, lingering distress and her urgent plea to the moon.
